title: How To Make Instant Dosa: The South Indian Classic Without Overnight Fermentation
excerpt: A combination of rice flour, semolina, yogurt and baking soda delivers crisp, golden dosas in under 30 minutes — no soaking or waiting required.
body:
• Instant dosa skips the overnight fermentation of traditional South Indian dosa by using a combination of rice flour, semolina and yogurt.
  • The batter needs just 15-20 minutes of resting time before it is ready to cook, making it practical for weekday breakfasts.
  • A small amount of baking soda provides the lift that fermentation would normally deliver, while yogurt adds the characteristic tang.
  • The result is a crisp, golden dosa that pairs well with coconut chutney and sambar — without the day-ahead planning.

The traditional South Indian dosa is a labor of love. Rice and urad dal are soaked for hours, ground into a fine batter and left to ferment overnight — a process that yields the characteristic tang and crispness that have made dosas one of India's most beloved breakfast staples. But for those short on time, the instant version offers a remarkably close approximation with a fraction of the effort, according to food publication Slurrp.

How It Works

The instant dosa batter relies on a trio of dry ingredients: rice flour, semolina (also called rava or suji) and a small amount of all-purpose flour. The semolina provides texture and crunch, the rice flour contributes the familiar dosa flavor, and the all-purpose flour helps bind the batter together. Yogurt replaces the tang that fermentation would normally produce, while a pinch of baking soda provides the lift.

"How It Works The instant dosa batter relies on a trio of dry ingredients: rice flour, semolina (also called rava or suji) and a small amount of all-purpose flour."

The ingredients are whisked together with water until smooth and pourable, then left to rest for just 15 to 20 minutes — enough time for the semolina to absorb moisture and soften. Just before cooking, the baking soda and a couple of tablespoons of oil are folded in.

The Recipe

Combine one cup of rice flour, half a cup of semolina and a quarter cup of all-purpose flour in a mixing bowl. Stir in one cup of yogurt and gradually add about one and a half cups of water, whisking continuously to eliminate lumps. Mix in one finely chopped green chilli, a tablespoon of chopped coriander leaves and salt to taste. Let the batter rest for 15-20 minutes.

When ready to cook, gently stir in a quarter teaspoon of baking soda and two tablespoons of oil. Heat a non-stick or well-seasoned cast-iron tawa over medium heat. Grease lightly, pour a ladleful of batter and spread it thin in a circular motion. Drizzle oil around the edges and cook until the base turns golden and lifts away from the pan.

Why It Works Without Fermentation

Fermentation in traditional dosa batter serves two purposes: it develops flavor through lactic acid production and creates air bubbles that make the dosa light and crisp. The instant version shortcuts both. Yogurt, which is itself a fermented product, provides the acidity and tang. Baking soda, when it reacts with the yogurt's acid, generates carbon dioxide bubbles that mimic the aeration of natural fermentation.

The trade-off is subtle. A fermented batter develops deeper, more complex flavors over its resting period, and the natural gas production creates a slightly different texture — more airy, with tiny holes across the surface. The instant version tends to be denser and crisper, which many people actually prefer for a snack-style dosa.

Variations Worth Trying

Health-conscious cooks have been experimenting with the instant format. An oats dosa version, popular on food blogs, replaces some of the rice flour with ground rolled oats for added fiber and protein. Ragi (finger millet) flour dosas, a South Indian tradition in their own right, work particularly well in instant format — the millet flour's slightly nutty flavor pairs naturally with the yogurt tang, and the calcium-rich grain adds nutritional value, according to recipe site Tarla Dalal.

Serve the dosas hot with coconut chutney, tomato chutney or sambar. For a more substantial meal, pair with potato masala for a quick masala dosa — the instant batter handles fillings just as well as its fermented counterpart.
